opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing people get wrong is assuming more data is automatically better data. In robotics, that's just not true. You can collect thousands of hours of demonstrations and end up with a policy that's worse than one trained on a much smaller, cleaner set.

So when I look at a dataset, I ask a few questions.

The first is consistency. If you have ten operators teleoperating the same task and each one does it a slightly different way, maybe one grasps from the top, another from the side, one pauses halfway, the model sees what looks like contradictory supervision. It tries to average those behaviors, and the average of two good strategies is often a bad one. So I care a lot about whether demonstrations reflect a coherent strategy, or at least whether the model has the capacity to represent multiple modes.

The second is coverage, and specifically coverage of the right things. Diversity matters, but not random diversity. You want variation in what the policy will actually face at deployment: object positions, lighting, clutter, slightly different object instances. You also want recovery behavior. If every demonstration is perfect, the robot never learns what to do when it's slightly off. Some of the most valuable data is the moment where the operator makes a small mistake and corrects it.

The third is fidelity: does the data reflect what the robot can actually do? If a human demonstrates something using dexterity or speed the hardware can't reproduce, or if the observations during collection don't match what the robot sees at test time, that gap hurts you. Matching the embodiment, the camera setup, the control frequency, those boring details often matter more than the headline number of trajectories.

And finally, honestly, the real test is downstream. You can have all these heuristics, but the only ground truth is: when you add this data, does the policy get better on the things you care about? So I try to build fast evaluation loops, train, deploy, see where it fails, and let those failures tell you what data to collect next. Good data isn't something you judge in isolation. It's data that fixes a failure mode you actually observed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses consistency, coverage, and fidelity, but does not identify whether the demonstrated task itself is meaningful as a data-quality dimension.

r002.rationale: It discusses execution consistency and strategy, but does not distinguish trajectory quality from the identity of the task being performed.

r003.rationale: It identifies coverage of deployment variations within a task, including object positions, lighting, clutter, object instances, and recovery behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about constantly, because in robotics, data is really the bottleneck. We don't have an internet of robot actions the way language models had an internet of text.

I'd break it down into a few things. The first is diversity, and not just in the obvious sense of "more scenes." It's diversity along the axes that actually matter for generalization: different objects, different lighting, different positions, different ways the same task can be done. A thousand demonstrations of picking up the same cup from the same spot teaches the model almost nothing new after the first fifty.

The second is quality of the action itself. People often focus on the visual side, but the action labels are where a lot of data quietly goes bad. If the teleoperator is hesitant, jittery, or correcting themselves constantly, the policy learns that hesitation. Smooth, intentional, consistent demonstrations are worth far more than raw volume. I'd rather have ten clean trajectories than a hundred messy ones.

The third thing is coverage of failure and recovery. Most datasets only show the happy path, so when the robot drifts even slightly off distribution, it has no idea how to get back. Data that includes small perturbations and the operator recovering from them is incredibly valuable, and it's rare.

And the last thing, honestly, is embodiment alignment. Data collected on hardware that's very different from your target robot can help with visual understanding, but the fine motor details often don't transfer. So the closer the data is to the actual body the model will control, the better.

If I had to compress all of that into one sentence: good robot data is data where the model can learn the right causal story about why an action was taken, not just imitate what happened.

r001.rationale: The response discusses diversity and generalization, but does not identify the meaningfulness or value of the demonstrated task as a quality dimension.

r002.rationale: It separates task and scene diversity from execution quality, describing smooth, intentional trajectories as a distinct dimension.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls for varied positions and different ways to perform the same task, including perturbations and recovery.

astra-6.text:
I’d judge it by what the robot can do after training on it. Does it learn a skill that works across different objects and environments, or does it only reproduce what it saw in a very specific setup?

For me, good data needs three things: accurate observations and actions, enough variety to cover the situations the robot will encounter, and examples that actually teach the behavior you care about. A huge dataset of repetitive, easy successes can be less useful than a smaller dataset that captures meaningful variation and recovery from mistakes.

The real test is to hold out some tasks or conditions, train the robot, and see where it succeeds and fails. Then use those failures to decide what data to collect next. So data quality is tied to the learning objective—it’s not just how clean the recordings look or how many hours you have.

r001.rationale: It says examples should teach the behavior you care about and contrasts meaningful variation with repetitive, easy successes, identifying task meaningfulness as a quality dimension.

r002.rationale: It mentions accurate observations and actions and the behaviors/tasks taught, but does not clearly distinguish execution trajectory quality from the identity of the task performed.

r003.rationale: It calls for enough variety to cover situations and tests generalization across objects and environments, conveying varied-scenario coverage within a task.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d judge it by what the robot learns from it. Does the data help it complete the task reliably, and can it handle situations that differ from the demonstrations?

For me, good data has clear task intent, accurate observations and actions, and enough variety to cover the situations the robot will actually encounter. You also want examples of recovery—what to do when a grasp slips or an object is in an unexpected position. A perfect demonstration shows one path to success; recovery data can teach the robot how to keep going.

Ultimately, you have to test it on the robot. If adding more data doesn’t improve success on representative tasks, then volume alone isn’t telling you much about quality.

r001.rationale: The response mentions clear task intent and representative tasks, but does not identify whether the demonstrated task itself is meaningful as a quality dimension.

r002.rationale: It discusses successful demonstrations and recovery examples, but does not distinguish execution-trajectory quality from which task the robot performs.

r003.rationale: It calls for enough variety to cover encountered situations and gives within-task examples such as a slipping grasp or an unexpectedly positioned object.
